results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response:
The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004952 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database. The calyx is the part closest to the cortex and receives sensory interneuron afferents, the pedunculus is a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes, and the mushroom body lobe system consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch, which have different structures at different life stages.

VFB holds extensive data related to the mushroom body, including [602](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004952 "View "Neurons with some part in mushroom body" in VFB") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [176](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004952 "View "Parts of mushroom body" in VFB") parts of the mushroom body, and over 22,000 images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response:
In the adult Drosophila brain, there are several types of Kenyon cells, including alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells. These can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and others. Specifically, gamma Kenyon cells are known to exist, innervating only the gamma lobe in the adult. 

VFB holds information on gamma Kenyon cells, including images, subclasses, expression patterns, scRNAseq data, and transgene expression. For example, there are [3](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "View "List all available images of gamma Kenyon cell" in VFB") available images of gamma Kenyon cells, [10](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "View "Subclasses of gamma Kenyon cell" in VFB") subclasses, [23](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "View "Expression patterns overlapping gamma Kenyon cell" in VFB") expression patterns overlapping with gamma Kenyon cells, [6](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "View "scRNAseq data for gamma Kenyon cell" in VFB") scRNAseq datasets, and 23 transgene expressions in gamma Kenyon cells.

This information is based on VFB's neuron taxonomy summary, which references publications by Lee et al. (1999) and Aso et al. (2014).

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron. It has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer. This arrangement allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli. LPLC2 projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. Its activity elicits a jump escape response. LPLC2 is connected to various neurons, including adult cholinergic neurons, T5c neurons, and T5b neurons. 
[Image removed: LPLC2 neuron]
VFB holds information on 2,594 neuron types, including the LPLC2. AVAILABLE VFB DATA includes neuron profiles and connections for these types.

results.response:
Publications that describe the PPL1 dopaminergic neurons and their role in aversive memory include Aso et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; and Truman et al., 2023. The PPL1 dopaminergic neurons are involved in aversive memory and project to various parts of the mushroom body, including the tip of the alpha lobe, the tip of the alpha' lobe, the upper portion of the alpha lobe segment 2, alpha lobe segment 1 and the lower part of segment 2, and the pedunculus and spur, as described by Mao and Davis, 2009.
